::: {#thm-symmetric-inverse}
#### Symmetric relations are their own inverses

Let $R$ be a relation on a set $S$ (@rem-relation-on-set).
Then $R$ is symmetric (@def-symmetric-relation) if and only if $R^{-1} = R$ (@def-inverse-relation).

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

($\Rightarrow$)
Suppose $R$ is symmetric.
We show $R^{-1} = R$ by double inclusion (@thm-double-inclusion).

- Let $(a, b) \in R^{-1}$.
  Then $(b, a) \in R$, by the definition of $R^{-1}$.
  Since $R$ is symmetric, $(a, b) \in R$.
  So $R^{-1} \subseteq R$.
- Let $(a, b) \in R$.
  Since $R$ is symmetric, $(b, a) \in R$,
  so $(a, b) \in R^{-1}$, by the definition of $R^{-1}$.
  So $R \subseteq R^{-1}$.

($\Leftarrow$)
Suppose $R^{-1} = R$, and let $a \mathrel{R} b$.
Then $(b, a) \in R^{-1}$, by the definition of $R^{-1}$,
and $R^{-1} = R$, so $b \mathrel{R} a$.
So $R$ is symmetric.

:::

:::
